title: Getting around
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE PARTICLE PAIR L1 SHIPPED AND NEVER CONTRASTED. -e marks a DESTINATION or a static location — hakgyo-e gayo, jip-e isseoyo — and -eseo marks where an ACTION happens: hakgyo-eseo gongbuhaeyo. L1-M7 taught both without the law, and this is the module whose job forces it open, because a direction is a destination and a bus stop is a place where something happens.

-(eu)ro is this module's own particle and it means TOWARD: oenjjok-euro gaseyo, i-jjok-euro oseyo. Meet it as a third member of the -e / -eseo family rather than as an idiom. -kkaji, "up to" or "as far as", joins it for the span from here to there; its partner -buteo ("from") is named in usage and not shown.

RIDING TAKES AN OBJECT PARTICLE, and no English speaker guesses it: beoseu-reul tayo, jihacheol-eul tayo — literally "the bus, ride it" — where English rides ON a bus. Getting off is naerida, and it takes -eseo, because getting off happens somewhere. The two halves of every journey take different particles, and the reason is visible once it is pointed out.

Directions reuse M1's honorific imperative in the field — gaseyo, oseyo, doraseyo, geonneoseyo — chipped formal, because the listener is the one being honoured. Korean is VERB-FINAL, so a direction is one long adverbial chain with the verb at the end of it, which is exactly why the per-sentence bound climbs here.

eotteoke asks HOW, and it is the whole of the question a lost traveller needs: N-e eotteoke gayo? — how do I get to N? It is not a request and takes no juseyo; asking the way is a question, and the answer comes back as an imperative.

sentences.cue: How do I get to the station?

words.note: A rail or subway station, and a bus stop is a jeongnyujang — the two words are never swapped. Its particle shapes are all here because this is the module that contrasts them.
The question word for a method, and it sits right in front of the verb. The h in the middle is written and barely heard.

sentences.trap: -e and not -eseo, because the station is where you are GOING rather than where anything is happening. That is the whole law of the pair, and this sentence is the cleanest place to see it.
sentences.sound: YEO-ge eo-TTEO-ke KA-yo. eotteoke runs as three quick syllables.

variations.cue: How do I get to the school?
How do I get to the bus stop?

variations.changed: asking where rather than how, with L1-M7's eodi

mistake.why: A destination takes -e: Yeok-e eotteoke gayo?

sentences.usage: The first sentence to have ready in a city you do not know.
sentences.mnemonic: -e is where you are going. -eseo is where it happens.

words.note: oen plus jjok, 'side'. oreunjjok is the right, built the same way, and both take -euro to mean toward.
A third member of L1's -e and -eseo family: not a destination and not a place of action, but a DIRECTION. After a vowel it shortens to -ro.

sentences.trap: -euro is a direction and not a destination, so it says which way to head rather than where to end up. Yeok-euro gaseyo sends somebody toward the station; Yeok-e gaseyo sends them to it.
sentences.sound: OEN-jjo-geu-ro ka-SE-yo. The jj is tense, made with the throat tightened.

variations.changed: straight ahead, which needs no particle at all
a landmark to steer by rather than a turn

sentences.usage: Given as an answer, and heard far more often than said.

sentences.cue: Go straight, then turn at the crossroads.

words.note: An adverb and nothing else — no particle, no ending. It is the word every direction starts with, and M3's -go stacks what comes after it: jjuk gago.
Literally 'four street'. Turning is an action that happens there, which is why it takes -eseo and not -e.
The honorific imperative of dolda, to turn. M1's ending in the field, doing the ordinary work of directions.

sentences.trap: sageori-eseo and not sageori-e, because the turning HAPPENS at the crossroads rather than ending there. Every verb of doing takes -eseo, and every verb of going takes -e.
sentences.sound: jjook KA-go sa-geo-ri-e-seo TO-se-yo. M3's -go is stacking the two halves.

variations.changed: a direction instead of the turn verb

mistake.why: An action happens at -eseo: sageori-eseo doraseyo.

sentences.usage: A whole direction, given in one breath.

words.note: From the English word, said in three syllables, and taeksi beside it. It takes the OBJECT particle with tayo, which is the module's real surprise.
It takes what you ride as a direct OBJECT — beoseu-reul tayo, literally 'the bus, ride it'. English rides ON a bus; Korean simply rides it.

sentences.trap: -reul and never -e. An English speaker reaches for a preposition here every single time, and Korean has none to offer: the vehicle is the object of the verb.
sentences.sound: BEO-seu-reul TA-yo. The eu is the flat vowel, not an oo.

variations.changed: the subway, which ends in a consonant so the particle is -eul
the honorific imperative — given as advice

mistake.why: What you ride is an object: Beoseu-reul tayo.

sentences.usage: Answering how you get to work.
sentences.mnemonic: You do not ride ON it. You ride IT.

sentences.cue: I get off at the station.

words.note: The other half of every journey, and it takes -eseo because getting off HAPPENS at the station. tayo and naeryeoyo take different particles for a visible reason.

sentences.trap: Getting on takes an object and getting off takes a place. beoseu-reul tayo, jeongnyujang-eseo naeryeoyo — two halves of one trip, two different particles, and the law of §1 explains both.
sentences.sound: YEO-ge-seo NAE-ryeo-yo. The ryeo is one syllable.

variations.cue: I get off at the bus stop.

variations.changed: the honorific imperative, as an instruction

variations.cue: I get off at the crossroads.

mistake.why: Getting off happens somewhere: Yeok-eseo naeryeoyo.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody where to leave the bus.
sentences.mnemonic: On takes an object. Off takes a place.

sentences.cue: Is it far from here to the station?

words.note: The far end of a span. Its partner is -buteo, 'from', which this level does not show — -eseo does that job in a sentence like this one.
A descriptive verb like every other. gakkawoyo is 'is near', and the two are asked and answered as a pair.

sentences.trap: -eseo here is 'from' and not 'at', which is the same particle doing a second job. A span needs both ends and Korean marks them differently: -eseo on the start, -kkaji on the finish.
sentences.sound: YEO-gi-e-seo YEOK-kka-ji MEO-reo-yo. The kk is tense.

variations.cue: It's near from here to the station.
It's far from home to school.
How do I get as far as the station?

mistake.why: The far end of a span takes -kkaji: yeok-kkaji.

sentences.usage: Asked before deciding whether to walk.

words.note: geonneo-, to cross, plus -pyeon, side. It takes -e because being somewhere is a location and not an action.
The honorific imperative from the same stem. Cross the road and you are at the geonneopyeon — the two words are one family.

sentences.trap: -e and not -eseo, because isseoyo is being somewhere rather than doing something. Every sentence with isseoyo takes -e, without exception at this level.
sentences.sound: geon-neo-PYEO-ne i-SSEO-yo. The nn is held.

variations.cue: The station is on the other side.

variations.changed: the instruction that gets you there

mistake.why: isseoyo is a location: Geonneopyeon-e isseoyo.

sentences.cue: The bus stop is up ahead.

words.note: A bus stop, never a train station — that is the yeok. Its four particle shapes are here because a stop is somewhere you go, wait and get off.
Ahead, with dwi for behind — the pair sits alongside L1-M7's wi and yeop, and all four take -e the same way.

sentences.trap: ap-e is 'in front' relative to where you both are, not to the bus stop. Korean position words point from the SPEAKER unless a noun is named in front of them.
sentences.sound: jeong-nyu-JANG-eun A-pe i-SSEO-yo. The p of ap runs into the particle.

variations.cue: The bus stop is behind us.
I take the bus at the stop.

mistake.why: A location takes -e: Jeongnyujang-eun ap-e isseoyo.

sentences.usage: Given while pointing, and understood without the pointing.

words.note: Literally 'under-ground iron'. gicha is a train between cities, and the two are not the same thing in Korean any more than in English.
A descriptive verb, so nothing follows it. Its modifier is ppareun — ppareun gicha, a fast train.

sentences.trap: Nothing here says 'faster' — Korean states it flat and lets the choice supply the comparison. M9 is where a real comparative arrives; until then, two flat statements do the work.
sentences.sound: ji-ha-CHEO-ri ppal-LA-yo. The ll is held for two beats.

variations.changed: M3's cheap, on the other option

mistake.why: ppallayo is the whole predicate: Jihacheol-i ppallayo.

sentences.usage: Choosing between two ways of getting there.
sentences.mnemonic: Two flat statements do a comparison, until M9.

words.note: The demonstrative is written joined to its noun, because a bare i is the SUBJECT PARTICLE's key and would collide with it. yeogi-ro is the same -ro after a vowel.
The honorific imperative of oda, to come — M1's ending again. wayo is its plain -yo shape, which M3 met as wasseoyo in the past.

sentences.trap: Korean writes the demonstrative next to what it points at, and this course joins them with a hyphen for a reason the index forces: a bare i is already the subject particle, so i chaek written apart would put a particle where a word should be.
sentences.sound: i-JJO-geu-ro o-SE-yo. The jj is tense and the whole phrase runs level.

variations.changed: a side instead of a demonstrative
M1's yeogi, and -ro because it ends in a vowel

sentences.usage: Said by whoever is showing you in.

comprehensionPool.cue: How do I get to the station?
I get off at the station.
Is it far from here to the station?
The bus stop is up ahead.
I take the bus at the stop.
